title: Blackout in the bank queue in a 76-year-old man
desc: In this station the candidate takes a focused history and examination from Frank, a 76-year-old man brought to the ED after a sudden 30-second blackout while standing in a bank queue. The blackout had no warning and followed a few minutes of palpitations, and he recovered quickly and fully. He takes metoprolol and has a slow, regular pulse. In Part 2 the candidate interprets his observations, which include a symptomatic pause, his 12-lead ECG and his blood results. They then recognise complete heart block causing cardiac syncope, manage symptomatic bradycardia in the ED and explain the plan to Frank, who lives alone.
focus: Transient loss of consciousness: separating cardiac syncope from vasovagal syncope and seizure, recognising complete heart block and managing symptomatic bradycardia
stem: You are a final-year medical student on placement in the Emergency Department of a metropolitan hospital, working with the ED team. Frank, a 76-year-old man, was brought in by ambulance after he lost consciousness for a short time at the bank this morning. He is on a trolley in an acute bay with cardiac monitoring attached. A nurse is with you and will carry out your instructions.
tasks: Take a focused history from Frank and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining. Start any immediate management you think he needs as you go (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Frank's observations, his 12-lead ECG and his blood results. Interpret them, give your most likely diagnosis and differentials, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Frank, aged 76, a retired man who lives on his own. You are sitting up on the trolley and feel well now, but you are a bit embarrassed about all the fuss and quietly frightened. Answer clearly. Give the history below only when asked. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "I was brought in by ambulance because I had a funny turn when I was waiting in the line at the bank this morning. I feel a lot better now."

What happened (give when asked)

  • If asked exactly what happened: "I was standing in the line waiting for about 5 minutes and then I must have blacked out, because the next thing I knew, I was lying on the ground with lots of people standing around me."
  • You do not remember falling.
  • It happened about an hour ago. People at the bank called the ambulance. They told you that you were out for about 30 seconds.
  • This has never happened before.
  • "I've never had anything like this before, and I'm scared that it will happen again."

Before the blackout (give when asked)

  • A normal morning. You had breakfast and your usual cup of tea and water. It was not hot in the bank.
  • No warning: "One minute I was standing in line, and the next thing I knew I was lying on the ground."
  • No light-headedness, sweating, going pale, greying or blurring of vision, or muffled hearing beforehand.
  • Palpitations (only if asked about your heart or palpitations): "I did feel my heart jump a few beats a few minutes before it happened." This has never happened before.
  • No chest pain, back pain or tummy pain. No shortness of breath.
  • You were not upset or emotional, and you were not coughing or straining.
  • You do not get dizzy when you stand up.
  • No vomiting, diarrhoea or bleeding (no black or bloody bowel motions).
  • No strange smell or taste and no odd feeling rising up from your stomach (no aura).

During the blackout (what the bystanders told the paramedics)

  • You suddenly fell down. You were out for about 30 seconds.
  • If asked: you did not hit your head, as far as anyone saw. No jerking, no frothing at the mouth, no moaning, and you did not wet or soil yourself.

Afterwards

  • You came round quickly and felt okay, just embarrassed. You knew where you were straight away.
  • No confusion, no injuries, no bitten tongue and no sore muscles. No headache. If asked specifically about a head injury: "No, I don't think I hit my head. Nothing hurts."
  • No weakness, numbness, trouble speaking or change in vision since.

Past medical history

  • High blood pressure.
  • No operations and no hospital admissions.
  • If asked: no diabetes, no Parkinson's disease, no known heart problems, no epilepsy, no strokes.

Medications and allergies

  • Metoprolol 50 mg twice a day for blood pressure, started by your GP 6 months ago. You took this morning's tablet at 7 am as usual. No other medicines and nothing new since then.
  • No known allergies.

Family history

  • Your father died at 72 of prostate cancer.
  • Your mother died at 81 of pneumonia after a hip fracture.
  • No one in the family died suddenly or young from a heart problem.

Social history

  • You are independent: you do your own shopping, cooking and cleaning, and you drive your own car to the shops.
  • You live alone and get lonely. Your wife died 2 years ago of breast cancer.
  • You have never smoked. A glass of wine once a week. No other drugs.

Ideas, concerns and expectations

  • Ideas: "I suppose I just fainted. Maybe I stood too long."
  • Concerns: "I'm scared that it will happen again. I live by myself; if I went down at home, nobody would find me."
  • Expectations: you would like to know what caused it, and you were hoping to go home today.
  • Question to ask: "Is it my heart, doctor?"

During the station

  • About halfway through Part 1, whatever the candidate is doing, say: "Oh, I feel a bit funny again, light-headed, like my heart's skipping." The nurse then reports the monitor (below). After about 20 seconds say: "That's passing now. That was just like the bank, before I went down."

The nurse (played by the examiner)

  • Gives the observations and the bedside glucose when asked (see the Exam findings).
  • If asked for collateral history, relays the paramedic handover. A bystander said Frank "just dropped, like someone switched him off", with no shaking. He came round within about 30 seconds and was talking normally when the paramedics arrived. Paramedic observations: HR 36, BP 130/62, BGL 6.4 mmol/L.
  • If the candidate asks for a 12-lead ECG: "I did one at triage. I'll bring it to you shortly." The ECG is handed over in Part 2.
  • At the halfway episode: "The monitor showed a pause of about 4 seconds. His heart rate is now 30 and his BP is 94/52." When Frank says it is passing: "Rate's back to 34. BP 120/58."
  • If the candidate calls a rapid response or a senior: "The ED registrar is coming." If they ask for pacing pads or the defibrillator: "Pads are on and connected." If they ask for IV access: "He has an 18 G in the left arm, and bloods went at 10:25."
  • If atropine is ordered with a dose and route: "Given." His rate stays at 34, with no change. If no dose is given: "What dose would you like?"
  • If an isoprenaline or adrenaline infusion is ordered: "I'll draw it up. The registrar will check it with me when they get here."
  • If the candidate says to withhold metoprolol: "I'll chart it as withheld."
  • If the candidate asks for blood results: "They'll be available in Part 2."

Exam findings (the examiner gives these when the candidate says what they are examining)

  • General: alert, comfortable, pink and well perfused. Weight 78 kg.
  • Observations: RR 16, SpO2 97% on room air, BP 128/60 (lying), HR 34 regular, temperature 36.6 °C, pain 0/10, CRT 2 seconds. Bedside glucose 6.2 mmol/L.
  • Lying and standing BP (if asked): if the candidate wants to stand him, the nurse says: "I'm not comfortable standing him with a rate of 34 and pads on. Can we hold off?" No standing values are given. If the candidate still insists, the nurse repeats the concern and does not stand him.
  • Pulse: 34/min, regular, large volume. Radial pulses equal.
  • JVP: 3 cm above the sternal angle, with intermittent large (cannon) a waves.
  • Heart sounds: first heart sound varies in loudness from beat to beat. Normal second sound. No murmur, no added sounds. No carotid bruits.
  • Chest: clear, no crackles. Peripheries: warm, no ankle oedema.
  • Head, neck and injuries: no scalp haematoma, laceration or tenderness. Cervical spine non-tender with full painless movement. No tongue bite. No bruising or tenderness of the hips, wrists or face.
  • Neurological: GCS 15 (E4 V5 M6), oriented. Pupils equal and reactive. Cranial nerves normal. Tone, power, reflexes, sensation and coordination normal and symmetrical in the limbs. No pronator drift. Plantars flexor.
  • Abdomen: soft, non-tender, no pulsatile mass. Rectal examination (if asked): not needed, no history of bleeding.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self and role, confirms Frank's identity and gains consent before examining.
Acknowledges his embarrassment and his fear that it will happen again, uses plain language, and answers "Is it my heart?" honestly without false reassurance.
History
Establishes exactly what happened:

kids.x: Standing in the bank queue for about 5 minutes, then woke on the ground with people around him; does not remember falling (true loss of consciousness)
About an hour ago, lasting about 30 seconds according to bystanders, who called the ambulance
First ever episode

check.x: Asks what happened before the blackout:

kids.x: No warning: no light-headedness, sweating, pallor, or change in vision or hearing
Palpitations: felt his heart 'jump a few beats' a few minutes before, never before
No chest, back or abdominal pain and no breathlessness
No triggers: not exertional, no emotion, cough, straining or heat, and no dizziness on standing
Normal eating and drinking; no vomiting, diarrhoea or blood loss

check.x: Asks about the event itself from the witness account:

kids.x: Fell suddenly; no jerking, frothing, moaning or incontinence
Asks specifically about a head strike

check.x: Asks about afterwards and screens for seizure and neurological causes: quick full recovery, no confusion, tongue biting, sore muscles, injury or headache, no aura, and no focal weakness, speech or visual change.
Takes the past history: hypertension, no surgery or admissions, and asks about diabetes, Parkinson's disease and known heart disease (none).
Takes the medication and allergy history:

kids.x: Metoprolol, started 6 months ago (identifies the beta blocker as relevant to the blackout)
No known allergies

check.x: Asks about family history of sudden cardiac death (none), and gets the father's prostate cancer at 72 and the mother's pneumonia after a hip fracture at 81.
Takes the social history: independent, lives alone and lonely since his wife died 2 years ago, drives, never smoked, a glass of wine a week.
Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: thinks he fainted, is scared it will happen again with no one to find him, and hopes to go home today.
Examination
Asks for a full set of observations and a bedside glucose, and recognises the HR of 34 as a significant bradycardia (BP 128/60, glucose 6.2 mmol/L).
Confirms he is on continuous cardiac monitoring (already attached) and asks for a 12-lead ECG early in the station.
Examines the cardiovascular system:

kids.x: Pulse: 34/min, regular, large volume
JVP with cannon a waves, and a first heart sound that varies in loudness
Auscultates for the murmur of aortic stenosis (none heard)
Asks about postural symptoms and defers lying and standing BP because of the bradycardia and risk of a pause (credit deferral only; do not credit standing him)
kids.d: Do not credit a candidate who insists on standing him.

check.x: Looks for injury from the fall: scalp, face and cervical spine, tongue, hips and wrists (none).
Performs a brief neurological examination: GCS 15, pupils and a limb screen, with no focal deficit.
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: HR 30 to 34 is in the red zone at every check, which is a rapid response criterion. At 11:00 there was a symptomatic 4-second pause with systolic BP 94 (yellow zone) and the nurse concerned. The recovery to 120/58 does not make him safe.
Interprets the ECG:

kids.x: Regular P waves (about 84/min) and regular QRS complexes (about 32/min) with no relationship between them: P waves march through, so there is complete AV dissociation
Broad QRS (150 ms) with RBBB morphology and left axis deviation: indicates an infranodal (fascicular or ventricular) escape, so the block is below the AV node; this escape is slow and unreliable
No ST elevation (no inferior STEMI as a cause)
Names complete (third-degree) heart block

check.x: Interprets the bloods: normal potassium, magnesium and calcium (no electrolyte cause), troponin not raised on the first sample (repeat needed), normal TSH, normal Hb (no blood loss) and normal renal function.

Gives cardiac (arrhythmic) syncope due to complete heart block as the diagnosis. Supports it with sudden loss of consciousness for 30 seconds with no warning, palpitations beforehand, quick full recovery, a beta blocker and the ECG.

Names at least three differentials, each with a feature against it: vasovagal syncope (no prodrome or trigger), seizure (no jerking, tongue biting or post-ictal state), orthostatic hypotension (no postural symptoms; collapse not on rising), ventricular tachyarrhythmia or acute MI (ECG and troponin).
Management
Recognises symptomatic red zone bradycardia after syncope and escalates at once: rapid response or senior ED doctor to the bedside, resuscitation bay, continuous monitoring.
check.d: Credit if done in Part 1 or stated in Part 2.

check.x: Has transcutaneous pacing pads applied with the defibrillator at the bedside and confirms IV access.
check.d: Credit if done in Part 1 or stated in Part 2.

check.x: Withholds metoprolol and avoids any other drug that slows AV conduction.
check.d: Credit if done in Part 1 or stated in Part 2.

check.x: Follows the bradycardia algorithm for adverse features (syncope, pause, hypotension):
check.d: Credit if done in Part 1 or stated in Part 2.

kids.x: Atropine 0.5 to 0.6 mg IV, repeated to a maximum of 3 mg, while stating it is unlikely to work for a broad-complex (infranodal) escape
If there is no response or further pauses: isoprenaline or adrenaline infusion and/or transcutaneous pacing (with analgesia and sedation) as a bridge to temporary transvenous pacing

check.x: Refers urgently to cardiology for admission to CCU or a monitored bed and a permanent pacemaker; he is not for discharge.
Completes the work-up: a repeat hs-troponin at 2 hours (per the local accelerated pathway), an echocardiogram for structural heart disease, and keeping potassium and magnesium in the normal range.

Explains to Frank in plain words: his heart's electrical wiring is blocked so it beats too slowly; it is not a simple faint; he needs to stay in hospital for a pacemaker; his blood pressure tablet is stopped for now. Responds to his fear about living alone.
Safety netting
Sets in-hospital escalation triggers for the nurses: any light-headedness, near-faint or blackout, a pause on the monitor, a falling heart rate, systolic BP below 100, chest pain or breathlessness.
check.d: Credit from the management answer (Q3), or from Part 1 if the candidate gave the nurse triggers there.

check.x: Tells Frank in plain words that after he goes home he should call 000 for another blackout, a near-faint, chest pain or breathlessness. He should see his GP or the pacemaker clinic for redness, swelling or discharge at the wound, or a fever.
Advises no driving until cardiology clears him (after a pacemaker, Austroads advises private drivers not to drive for at least 2 weeks).

Arranges follow-up: pacemaker clinic check, a GP review of his blood pressure treatment without metoprolol, and support at home because he lives alone (a personal alarm, social work or community supports).

part2.lead: It is now 11:20. Here are Frank's observations since he arrived, the 12-lead ECG taken at triage, and his blood results.
part2.patient:
For the fourth question, Frank is calm but worried. As the candidate explains:

  • Ask once: "Will I still be able to drive?"
  • If the candidate mentions a pacemaker, ask: "A pacemaker? At my age? Is that a big operation?"
  • If the candidate uses jargon (heart block, AV node, bradycardia), ask: "What does that mean?"

When it is explained clearly, say: "Well, if it stops this happening again, I'd rather have it."

handover.label: Observations since arrival
handover.result: On continuous cardiac monitoring from triage. Room air throughout. GCS 15 at every check.
handover.model:
• Read: HR 34 regular at 10:15 and 10:45, 30 at 11:00 and 34 at 11:15: in the red zone at every check. At 11:00 there was a 4-second pause on the monitor with light-headedness, and systolic BP 94 (yellow zone) with the nurse concerned. During the pause CRT lengthened to 3 s with mild distress, both resolving by 11:15, consistent with transient hypoperfusion. BP is otherwise 120 to 128 systolic with a wide pulse pressure. RR, SpO2 and temperature are white throughout, he is alert, and the glucose is normal.
  • Meaning: a persistent, symptomatic bradycardia with pauses that reproduce his presenting symptoms. The escape rhythm is unreliable, so another pause could cause syncope or asystole.
  • Changes: a red zone heart rate is a rapid response criterion (in ED, immediate senior review in the resuscitation bay). The yellow zone BP and nurse concern add to it. He needs continuous monitoring, pacing pads on, the senior at the bedside and urgent cardiology. Recovery between episodes does not make him safe.

rows.note: Triage: blackout at bank. Cardiac monitor attached, 12-lead ECG requested
Feels well. Seen by ED team
Light-headed, 'heart skipping'. 4-second pause on monitor. Doctor at bedside
Symptoms settled after about 20 seconds. Remains on continuous monitoring

handover.label: 12-lead ECG (10:20, triage)
handover.result:
12-lead ECG, 25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV, taken at 10:20. Frank, 76, after a blackout.

  • Rate: atrial rate 84/min; ventricular rate 32/min.
  • Rhythm: P waves regular (constant PP interval). QRS complexes regular (constant RR interval). No consistent relationship between P waves and QRS complexes: P waves fall at varying points before, within and after the QRS complexes and T waves.
  • PR interval: varies from beat to beat; no fixed PR interval.
  • Axis: left axis deviation (about −60°).
  • QRS: broad, 150 ms. rSR' pattern in V1 with broad, slurred S waves in I and V6.
  • QT: 560 ms; QTc 410 ms (Bazett).
  • ST segments and T waves: no ST elevation or depression. T-wave inversion in V1 to V3, in keeping with the QRS morphology. No pathological Q waves.
  • Comparison: no previous ECG available.
  • Conclusion: complete (third-degree) AV block with a regular broad-complex escape rhythm at 32/min (RBBB morphology, left axis deviation). No acute ST changes.
handover.model:
• Read: atrial rate 84 and ventricular rate 32, both regular but independent of each other. P waves march through the QRS complexes and T waves with no fixed PR interval, so there is complete AV dissociation. A broad QRS (150 ms) with RBBB morphology and left axis deviation indicates an infranodal (fascicular or ventricular) escape, so the block is below the AV node. This escape is slow and unreliable. No ST elevation and no Q waves. The QTc is normal.
  • Meaning: complete (third-degree) heart block with a slow, broad-complex infranodal escape. This explains a sudden blackout without warning (Stokes-Adams attack), the palpitations, the cannon a waves and the variable first heart sound. Disease below the AV node is unstable and carries a risk of asystole. Metoprolol may have unmasked it, but stopping it is unlikely to restore reliable conduction.
  • Changes: pacing pads on, avoid AV nodal blockers, and expect atropine to be ineffective. Chronotropic infusion or pacing if there are further pauses. Urgent cardiology for temporary and then permanent pacing. No STEMI, but repeat the troponin.

handover.label: Blood results
handover.result: Collected 10:25 at cannulation. Troponin is the 0-hour sample; repeat due 12:25.
handover.model:
• Read: FBC normal (Hb 142). Sodium, potassium 4.3, magnesium 0.86, corrected calcium 2.36, glucose 6.2, urea and creatinine (eGFR 68) normal. High-sensitivity troponin T 11 ng/L, below the 99th percentile. TSH normal.
  • Meaning: no reversible cause for the heart block. There is no hyperkalaemia, no hypermagnesaemia, no hypothyroidism and, so far, no evidence of myocardial infarction. A normal Hb argues against blood loss as a cause of collapse.
  • Changes: the only possible contributing factor is metoprolol, which is withheld. Repeat hs-troponin at 2 hours (per the local accelerated pathway). Keep potassium and magnesium normal. Renal function is adequate for contrast if angiography is needed.

ask: You are now calling the cardiology registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Frank, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Frank now, here in the emergency department.
Frank asks you, "Is it my heart, and can I go home today?" Please answer him, including what he should watch out for and the follow-up he will need.
expect:
• Identify: self, medical student with the ED team; Frank, 76.
  • Situation: syncope from complete heart block with a broad-complex escape at 30 to 34/min, and a symptomatic 4-second pause at 11:00.
  • Background: sudden 30-second blackout standing in a queue, no warning, palpitations minutes before, quick full recovery, no seizure features or head strike; first episode; hypertension on metoprolol for 6 months; no allergies; lives alone.
  • Assessment: HR 34 (red zone), BP 128/60 falling to 94/52 during the pause, GCS 15; cannon a waves, variable S1, no murmur. ECG: P waves 84 dissociated from a broad infranodal escape at 32 with QRS 150 ms, RBBB morphology and left axis deviation, no STEMI. Electrolytes, TSH and Hb normal; troponin 11, repeat due.
  • Recommendation: please review now; pads on, metoprolol withheld; advice on atropine or isoprenaline; temporary pacing if needed; CCU admission and permanent pacemaker.

Cardiac (arrhythmic) syncope from complete heart block: sudden loss of consciousness for 30 seconds with no warning, palpitations beforehand, quick full recovery, on a beta blocker, HR 34 with cannon a waves, and an ECG with AV dissociation and a broad escape.

  • Vasovagal syncope: for: standing in a queue; against: no prodrome, trigger or pallor, and the ECG.
  • Orthostatic hypotension (drug-induced): for: on an antihypertensive, standing; against: no dizziness on standing, collapsed after standing still for 5 minutes rather than on rising, and the ECG shows another cause.
  • Seizure: against: no jerking, incontinence, tongue biting or post-ictal confusion; rapid recovery.
  • Ventricular tachyarrhythmia: for: palpitations, sudden collapse; against: no VT seen on the ECG or monitor.
  • Acute MI (inferior) causing heart block: against: no chest pain, no ST elevation, troponin not raised (repeat pending).

1. Resus bay, monitoring, senior at bedside, pads on, IV access.
  2. Withhold metoprolol; no other AV nodal blockers.
  3. Adverse features (syncope, pauses, hypotension): atropine 0.5 to 0.6 mg IV, repeated to a maximum of 3 mg. It is likely to fail with a broad escape.
  4. If there are further pauses or hypotension: isoprenaline or adrenaline infusion titrated to rate, and/or transcutaneous pacing with analgesia and sedation, as a bridge to temporary transvenous pacing.
  5. Urgent cardiology: admit to CCU or a monitored bed for a permanent pacemaker.
  6. Repeat hs-troponin at 2 hours (per the local accelerated pathway), echocardiogram, keep K and Mg normal.
  7. Escalation triggers for nursing staff: any light-headedness, near-faint or blackout, a pause on the monitor, HR falling below 30, SBP below 100, chest pain or breathlessness. Call the senior/MET at once.

• Plain words: yes, it is your heart. Its electrical wiring is blocked, so it beats too slowly and sometimes pauses, and that made you black out. It was not a simple faint. Your blood pressure tablet is stopped, but the wiring problem won't go away by itself.
  • Today: not safe to go home. Stay on the heart monitor; a pacemaker is a small procedure, a device put under the skin, usually under local anaesthetic.
  • After discharge: call 000 for another blackout, near-faint, chest pain or breathlessness; see the GP or pacemaker clinic for wound redness, swelling, discharge or fever.
  • Driving: not until cardiology clears him, at least 2 weeks after a pacemaker.
  • Follow-up: pacemaker clinic, GP for blood pressure medicines, a personal alarm or community support as he lives alone.

ddx.dx: Cardiac (arrhythmic) syncope due to complete heart block
ddx.for: A sudden 30-second blackout with no warning, palpitations minutes before, quick full recovery, on metoprolol, HR 34 with cannon a waves, and an ECG showing AV dissociation with a broad infranodal escape.
He had been standing in a queue for about 5 minutes.
ddx.against: He had no prodrome (no light-headedness, sweating, pallor or visual greying), no emotional or situational trigger, and his ECG shows complete heart block.

ddx.for: He takes an antihypertensive and was standing when he collapsed.
ddx.against: No dizziness on standing, and he collapsed while standing still rather than on rising; postural BP deferred because of the bradycardia.

ddx.for: He had a sudden loss of consciousness and does not remember falling.
ddx.against: There was no jerking, frothing, incontinence, tongue biting, sore muscles or post-ictal confusion, he had no aura, and he recovered within seconds.

ddx.for: He had palpitations before a sudden collapse without warning.
ddx.against: The monitor and ECG show a slow escape rhythm with no ventricular tachycardia, and he has no family history of sudden cardiac death.

ddx.dx: Acute (inferior) myocardial infarction causing AV block
ddx.for: He is 76 and hypertensive, with new complete heart block.
ddx.against: He had no chest pain or breathlessness, the ECG has no ST elevation or Q waves, and the first troponin is not raised (repeat pending).

guide:
This is an acute station. In Part 1 the examiner also plays the nurse. Give the observations and glucose when asked, relay the paramedic handover if asked for collateral, and give findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. If a 12-lead ECG is requested, say it was done at triage and will come in Part 2. If the candidate asks to stand him for a postural BP, the nurse objects as scripted and no standing values are given; credit item 17.4 only for deferring it. About halfway, whatever the candidate is doing, Frank reports light-headedness and the nurse reports a 4-second pause with HR 30 and BP 94/52. It settles after about 20 seconds regardless of treatment. Atropine, if ordered with a dose, produces no change in rate. An isoprenaline or adrenaline infusion is drawn up but not yet running by Part 2. Credit escalation, pads and IV access (items 27 and 28), and withholding metoprolol and atropine (items 29 and 30), whether they are done in Part 1 or stated in Part 2.

In Part 2, read the lead, hand over all three results together, then ask the four questions in order. The ECG is interpreted within the ISBAR; credit item 22 from that answer or from the diagnosis answer. Credit item 35 from the management answer (Q3), or from Part 1 if the candidate gave the nurse triggers there. For the fourth question, the person playing Frank asks the questions in the Part 2 script.

A high-performing candidate establishes true loss of consciousness, then works systematically through before, during and after. They draw out the absence of a prodrome, the palpitations, the lack of seizure features and the absence of a head strike, and they find the beta blocker. They feel a pulse of 34 and act on it: monitor, ECG, pads and a senior. In Part 2 they read complete heart block from the ECG, note the broad escape and the pause, withhold metoprolol, and know that atropine may fail and that pacing is the answer. They do not let him go home.

A borderline candidate takes a generic falls or seizure history, misses the palpitations or the metoprolol, does not act on the heart rate, calls the ECG "bradycardia" or first-degree block, or plans discharge with GP follow-up.
explain:
Diagnosis: cardiac syncope from complete heart block

Syncope is a transient loss of consciousness from global cerebral hypoperfusion, with rapid onset, short duration and spontaneous complete recovery. Frank was standing in a queue when he lost consciousness with no warning. He felt his heart "jump a few beats" minutes before, was out for about 30 seconds, and recovered quickly and fully. Sudden syncope without a prodrome, preceded by palpitations, in an older man on a beta blocker, is arrhythmic until proven otherwise. His slow, regular, large-volume pulse, cannon a waves (the atrium contracting against a closed tricuspid valve) and a first heart sound that varies in loudness are the bedside signs of AV dissociation. A sudden blackout from a bradyarrhythmia like this is called a Stokes-Adams attack.

Taking a transient loss of consciousness history

  • Establish true loss of consciousness: are they sure? Do they remember falling? Was it a trip or a fall without blackout?
  • Exactly what happened, including position and activity. Syncope on exertion suggests outflow obstruction (aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy) or arrhythmia. Syncope when lying down suggests arrhythmia.
  • Before: prodrome (light-headedness, sweating, nausea, visual greying, muffled hearing), triggers (prolonged standing, heat, emotion, pain, cough, micturition, straining), palpitations, chest pain, breathlessness, aura, intake and fluid or blood loss.
  • During, from a witness: duration, colour, jerking, frothing, moaning, incontinence, head strike.
  • After: speed of recovery, confusion, tongue biting, sore muscles, headache, injuries.
  • Medications (antihypertensives, AV nodal blockers, QT-prolonging drugs), cardiac history, diabetes and Parkinson's disease (autonomic failure), family history of sudden cardiac death. Always ask about injuries and head strike.

Differentials

  • Vasovagal syncope: a trigger and a prodrome of warmth, sweating, nausea and pallor, then a brief fall with quick recovery, sometimes with fatigue afterwards. Frank had neither a trigger nor a prodrome.
  • Orthostatic hypotension: on standing up, in people with volume depletion, antihypertensives or autonomic failure. A fall in systolic BP of 20 mmHg or more, or diastolic of 10 or more, within 3 minutes of standing.
  • Seizure: lateral tongue biting, prolonged jerking, head turning, an aura, and post-ictal confusion and drowsiness. A few brief myoclonic jerks can happen in syncope, so a witness account matters.
  • Structural heart disease: aortic stenosis gives exertional syncope and an ejection systolic murmur; Frank has no murmur.
  • Ventricular arrhythmia and acute coronary syndrome: must be excluded with the ECG, monitoring and troponin. An inferior MI can cause AV block, usually at the level of the node and with a narrow escape.

Every patient with transient loss of consciousness needs a 12-lead ECG. Features of high-risk syncope include no prodrome, syncope on exertion or lying down, palpitations beforehand, known structural heart disease, a family history of sudden death, and an abnormal ECG.

Interpreting the results

AV blockECG
First degreePR above 200 ms, every P conducted
Second degree, Mobitz I (Wenckebach)PR lengthens progressively until a P is dropped
Second degree, Mobitz IIConstant PR with sudden dropped P waves; often with a broad QRS
Third degree (complete)No P waves conducted: regular P waves and a regular, slower escape rhythm, independent of each other
  • ECG: P waves at 84/min march through the QRS complexes at 32/min with no fixed PR interval, which is complete heart block. A narrow escape (junctional, 40 to 60/min) suggests block at the AV node. Frank's broad escape (150 ms, RBBB morphology, left axis deviation) is most likely infranodal (fascicular/ventricular), from below the AV node: slow, unreliable and prone to pauses and asystole.
  • Observations: HR 30 to 34 sits in the red zone of the NSW Between the Flags chart throughout, which is a rapid response criterion. The 11:00 pause, with symptoms and a yellow zone BP, shows the escape rhythm failing.
  • Bloods: look for reversible causes, such as hyperkalaemia, hypothyroidism, ischaemia and drug toxicity. Frank's are normal, so the beta blocker is the only contributor found.

Management (ANZCOR bradycardia guidance; eTG Cardiovascular)

  • Continuous cardiac monitoring in a resuscitation area, IV access, senior review, and transcutaneous pacing pads with the defibrillator at the bedside.
  • Adverse features (syncope, shock, myocardial ischaemia, heart failure) call for treatment. Atropine 0.5 to 0.6 mg IV, repeated to a maximum of 3 mg. Atropine acts on the AV node, so it often fails in complete heart block with a broad escape.
  • If there is no response, or there is a risk of asystole (complete heart block with a broad QRS, Mobitz II, recent asystole, ventricular pauses over 3 seconds): an isoprenaline or adrenaline infusion titrated to heart rate, and/or transcutaneous pacing with analgesia and sedation, as a bridge to temporary transvenous pacing.
  • Withhold the beta blocker and other AV nodal blockers (non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, digoxin). A beta blocker at a normal dose often unmasks existing conduction disease rather than causing it, so conduction frequently stays abnormal after the drug is stopped.
  • Urgent cardiology referral: admit to CCU or a monitored bed. Symptomatic complete heart block that is not from a reversible cause is an indication for a permanent pacemaker. Echocardiography assesses structural disease and LV function.

Safety netting, driving and living alone

On the ward, nurses escalate any light-headedness, near-faint or blackout, pauses, a falling heart rate or BP, chest pain and breathlessness. After a pacemaker, Frank needs a pacemaker clinic check. He should see his GP or the pacemaker clinic for wound redness, swelling, discharge or fever. He should call 000 for another blackout, chest pain or breathlessness. Under Austroads, he must not drive until cleared; after pacemaker insertion private drivers should not drive for at least 2 weeks. His GP needs to review his blood pressure treatment without metoprolol. Because he lives alone and is lonely, discuss a personal alarm, community supports and social work before discharge.
points: In transient loss of consciousness, first establish that consciousness was truly lost. Then take the history before, during and after the event, including the witness account and a question about head strike and injuries.
No warning, palpitations beforehand, syncope on exertion or lying down, structural heart disease and an abnormal ECG mean cardiac syncope until proven otherwise. Every blackout needs a 12-lead ECG.
Syncope and seizure differ: seizure brings prolonged jerking, tongue biting, an aura and post-ictal confusion, while syncope brings quick, complete recovery.
In complete heart block, P waves march through a slower, independent escape rhythm. A broad-complex escape most likely arises below the AV node and is unstable.

For symptomatic bradycardia: monitor, apply pacing pads and give atropine 0.5 to 0.6 mg IV (up to 3 mg), knowing it often fails with a broad escape. Move to an isoprenaline or adrenaline infusion or pacing, withhold AV nodal blockers, and refer to cardiology for a permanent pacemaker.
Safety netting covers 000 for another blackout, no driving until cleared under Austroads, and support for an older person who lives alone.
